David French’s column leaves me with a profound sense of sadness.

I am 81 years old, descended from English colonists whose American story reaches back to the Revolutionary era. I have spent most of my life proud of what this imperfect nation accomplished over nearly 250 years. Yet increasingly I begin my mornings embarrassed by what I see happening to my country.

French’s examples are difficult to dismiss: depleted stocks of critical weapons, strained alliances, experienced military leaders being pushed aside and an Army left with crucial leadership positions unfilled. Most troubling is his warning that competence and independence within the military are increasingly giving way to loyalty and sycophancy.

This goes beyond any single general or defense secretary. For me, it raises a much larger and more painful question about the country itself.

I grew up believing that American greatness rested not simply on military or economic power, but on strong institutions, competent public servants, dependable alliances and respect for facts. Reading this column, I find myself wondering what has happened to those values.

After eight decades of being proud to call myself an American, that is a deeply sad question to have to ask.

comments.body:
I kept a journal for many years. I did write about struggles and disagreements with my late wife, among many other matters. Just writing it out helped me to better understand what was bothering me, and sometimes where I myself was the one falling short.

I wrote it on my personal laptop. I had complete trust that she respected my privacy. And I respected hers. I would never have dreamed of reading her emails, text messages, or contents on her computer without her permission. Even when I did happen to know her PINs and passwords--that access was for emergencies, not snooping.

I did not regard that as "keeping secrets from me." Rather, we both had private spaces where we could work through our own thoughts and feelings with complete privacy. I trusted her to tell me anything I needed to know. I trusted that she shared her whole heart with me, just as I shared mine with her.

So, in my marriage, the snooping that the husband did would have been a breach of trust that would have compounded any problems we were already working through.

At the same time, I think that when the wife shared extracts from her journal during couple's therapy, that compounded their problems in a different way. Credit her with good intentions, to provide more context about her thinking at the times these incidents occurred. It's still completely understandable that her husband felt like she was litigating these past incidents, that she had stored up resentments to brood on them. What a mess.

In the eighteenth-century Carolina wilderness, reportedly, a person approaching the home of a stranger was supposed to shout, "Hello, the house!" How far we've come.

GenZ is not the only generation to blame when it comes to using their phones to carry out the silent treatment.  In couples therapy, the silent treatment is still referred to as a form of abuse. In my own generation, bitter Boomer family members use the same technology to shun members of their own family.

What these Boomers have in common with GenZ non-responders is the impossibility of resolving disputes or forging new bonds via discourse. It's a reminder that customary greetings like "hello" and "goodbye," even bowing or shaking hands,  emerged as a way of helping individuals indicate their membership in a group or class, like curtseying before the queen.  Just because these traditions that facilitated communication have disappeared does not mean that the differences they are meant to overcome have done the same.

comments.name: Jeannine Bonesteele

This is all very interesting. I’ve been using ChatGPT as a virtual “financial advisor” for about 18 months, and it has helped me make some great decisions on managing my portfolio, but nothing as sophisticated as what is suggested in this article. But obviously the more recent agentic capabilities becoming more widely available, and advances in AI capabilities in general with Claude and now ChatGPT Astra, are rapidly changing what is possible. I intend still to approach this cautiously. I don’t intend to give an AI agent direct access to my accounts where it can perform independent trades. I need to remain the “human in the loop” strictly for security reasons … the potential cost of an AI running amok with full privileges in my retirement accounts could be disastrous. So, I’d first construct a pipeline that generates analysis and recommendations, with asynchronous notifications of thresholds and events that trigger pre-staged decisions. But at least for now, I want to be the entity that executes those recommended actions. Also, as I’ve found during the past 18 months, the AI is only as trustworthy as the data source it can access … because it tends to ‘fabricate’ data that it can’t access while hallucinating that it retrieved good data (aka ‘lying’). So I’d want to ensure my agent has a reliable pipeline to real, verifiable data. AI can become a VERY powerful tool in assisting me in managing my portfolio, but ‘trustworthy’ isn’t yet a word I’d use regarding AIs.

High School. American History class. 

I had a teacher like Mr. Wolfson. And without him, I wouldn't have lived the life I have. Then, it was a life I could only imagine.

My teacher was Mr. Armstrong. He was the AP U.S. history teacher. I was the only kid in the class who came from a working class background. The rest of the kids were upper middle class - vacations in Europe each summer, new cars, beautiful homes, tutors for every subject. They had everything I didn't have. But I soon realized this: I might not ever have what they had, but I could know what they knew. 

I was soon one of the best students in the class. How did that happen? A good teacher makes students want to work hard. 

Mr. Armstrong encouraged me, took the time to have real talks with me, about what I would study in college, assuming I could afford college anywhere. In 1971 he told me I should consider being a lawyer. Me. A young ethnic girl from a working class background. But he told me I could do this. And when I got the highest score in his class on the AP test, he was thrilled. I honestly think he was happier than I was.

Five years later I started law school.

It takes only one person to believe in a child. One teacher. That's all it took. I wouldn't be who I am, or where I am, without his support.

OC

The governance structure needs to look like more like automated institutions that govern society within an AI run time environment.

This could include  agents that effectively police other agents that are created, and hard boundaries on what is illegal, or immoral.  This run time environment should have an international component that all countries agree on and any AI system must deploy this.  Country and state laws layer under that.  
Professional societies could have their own layer to enforce their professional ethics.

The author may be right that social science needs more public funding, but the piece is unconvincing special pleading. She concedes that industry-funded research may be rigorous and objects only that companies shape the questions. The NSF does this too, through program officers and peer review panels with their own well-documented biases, and a decade of replication failures shows that academic incentives are no guarantee of truth. The choice is not between pure and captured research but between one funder and many, and a plurality of funders is the healthier system.

Commercial research operates under a discipline the academy lacks: a result that doesn't hold up costs money. In my own field, biomedicine, Amgen scientists reported in 2012 that they could reproduce only six of fifty-three landmark preclinical cancer papers, and Bayer found similar rates. Industry researchers' frustration with unreliable academic work is not new. Nor is the academy's tendency to drift from broader public values; social psychologists themselves have documented how their field's political homogeneity distorts what gets studied and what is believed. The academy has never had a monopoly on truth, and the AI companies now hiring social scientists, philosophers and psychologists are more likely to widen the conversation than to narrow it.

The below includes some violence.

The big question, for me, isn’t how people get into an abusive relationship, but how do they safely get out of it.  I found out that my older sister was in an abusive marriage, on the morning after she told her husband that she was leaving him.  He, then, went back into the bedroom, got out his shotgun and blew my sister’s head off, and, then, about three minutes later, blew his own head off.

This was in the late ‘70s, before there were enough companies around to clean up after something like this.  So my younger sister, myself, and a couple of friends, had to go in and clean up the apartment.  I still can close my eyes and see what I saw when I pulled a chunk of her skull, with hair and some of her brains attached, out from behind some books.  It is almost 50 years later, and, while we have made progress, this is still happening among us, albeit, at a lower rate.  I understand on an intellectual level why this still might happen, but on an emotional level, it still rises up and screams in my head, asking why I still read and hear about such abuse.

I had to ask myself, before I signed up for the USAF (knowing my draft notice arrived at home) and found myself in the Vietnam War, could I kill someone?  The answer was (and still is) that I could, but only when confronting someone who is violent and threatening me or others.  And, on a philosophical level, I see the similarity, and the larger difference, between me and my brother-in-law.

Lansing is similar to other small NC communities like Crossnore and Penland, which strive to keep local arts and heritage alive and help provide mountain residents with a means to stay employed. The students at the weaving school at Crossnore produce amazing fiber arts and attire with scarcely any recognition. Check it out if you plan traveling to the Boone, Blowing Rock or Linville area.

Asheville gets most of the attention in NC because it is hip and on everyone's radar. The small communities in outlying areas like these deserve attention, too.

In July, NYT had an article about the return of the grandma hobbies, especially among our young people. https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/18/well/grandma-hobbies-crafts-knitting-quilting.html

An interesting piece of info is that communities are creating makeshift lodgings [a tent, a renovated school bus, a tiny house ] for guests -- yes some New Yorkers pre-approved not to be obnoxious might arrive -- who come to communities like this one to attend a class for the week or weekend. It's not fancy but very rewarding to those who participate. 

I'm dealing with this global trend being advanced by one company in particular called Golden Goose, operating out of Italy, but they just opened a 4,000 sq ft shopping/learning store in Houston. They're Polo Ralph Lauren pricepoints, but the point is that the shoemakers are on the location right in the store, and the buyer learns how the shoes are made and also helps design them. 

I don't want to dump luxury world ideas on this simple concept with substance. I'm only saying that this story is part of a much larger trend that values what is being done in a "small mountain town".  This is not a political statement but NC resident Anderson Clayton comes to mind. She could do amazing outreach on a project like this one. What I'm saying is "do it yourselves and bravo to you" -- but something even more significant in terms of income and grants may be out there, because there's a lot of respect turning towards ideas and communities like yours.

There is a great program in Hindman Ky called Culture of Recovery. It is run by a master luthier and connected to the Appalachian Artisan Center locating nearby. Totally flooded although they saved some of the historic instruments, especially dulcimers which the program makes. Lost much of the little factory. Have rebuilt the program and  Troublesome Creek Stringed Instrument Company, a non-profit factory in an old school. Local people, local woods, local history preserved. They make several instruments but specialize in the mountain dulcimer native to the area.

comments.body:
I appreciate comments that note community colleges are an option, and high school students need better financial literacy, etc.  But at a certain point those comments ignore the issue. 

Reality is that a firmly established middle class family in America can have an incredibly motivated, intelligent, mature, industrious teenager that has worked part time jobs, learned personal finance, manged their own bank account, excelled academically, etc. This family may have managed their assets very wisely, drive old cars, save consistently, and avoid unnecessary purchases.  And this family can still be looking at utterly unmanageable astronomic costs to send their prepared and motivated child to college. That is absolutely BONKERS in the land of abundance and needs to change. Colleges and universities need to lower their prices. Families shouldn't have to do ridiculous gymnastics to figure out how to afford it.

She's the real hero around here!

comments.name: Katie
comments.body:
Our young people deserve better. They deserve what the generations before them had - a much more affordable college experience, even with some debt - and they're not getting it. 

As someone who, for years, as a volunteer, counselled seniors in high school on how to fill out college applications and apply for scholarships, I don't think I can even recommend state schools in Oregon anymore unless the kid has family money to put toward the cost or they have a huge scholarship.

Oregon State and University of Oregon are, exactly as this articles states - $38,000 a year. Almost every one of my students was a kid of color, first generation, had immigrant parents, etc. so they qualified for scholarships. However, even if they had excellent grades,  we were only looking at about $7,000 in scholarships. 

I worked all through college, and I told my students they should expect to, also. So, let's say they can throw $5,000 at that cost for a total of $12,000. 

They're still looking $26,000 a year. A minimum, if costs don't rise one cent, of $104,000 loan. That's horrible.

The best way now, for kids with no family money, is a community college AND taking as many classes at high school where you can get community college credit. 

The last two years, head to a state school.

If kids get into Ivy League schools that will pay the whole thing, awesome. That just isn't going to happen for the majority. 

We used to invest in our young people. No more. We just saddle them with debt.

comments.name: populistcurious
comments.body:
Whenever I read one of these stories about people having problems with loans I always want to know how much. Show me the money. How much did they borrow at what percent, how much were they paying back per month. 

I want to know to see if payments are as large as a mortgage, because they should be. No one should owe money for very long at all. Many with student loans borrow to pay living expenses, which is not a good idea. Live with the folks and commute. 

Tuition and fees at Oregon State for a typical academic years is around $16K. So the same exact mistake is being made again, and I'm expected to pay for it. I'm not an "educator" like the fellow in the story, I worked all my life doing hard labor, and I put two kids through college. I know how to save and invest money, a skill anyone headed to college should learn.

Go to nerd wallet. Do the math. I'm sick of paying for people who refuse to exercise basic self discipline.

You know, I always read these articles and usually save them.  Some have been added into my rotation of workouts .  What I should do - but haven’t - is added up the time needed to do all the exercises that have been written about in the NYT over the last 4 years.  There’s rotational strength, grip strength, core, glutes, lateral moves, jump roping, shoulder pain prevention, stronger hips, balance + (strength, coordination, etc), and many more. 

I’m pretty sure if I add up all of them, there’d be little time left for me to keep building my concentration and focus, memorize some poetry, do the 10-minute stare at a painting, enjoy 6 things, etc.  Not to mention laundry, cleaning kitty litter boxes, reading a few books now and then, getting to in the garden, learning a few new things each week (the exercises might stand in for that?) etc.

It’s the rare cookbook where I cook even 1/4 of the recipes, but I find a few favorites, read the others and extract info that I might use from time to time, and don’t lose any sleep (gotta get those 7 to 8 good hours in) over the rest.

comments.name: Nogi Ichida
comments.body:
I can’t really think how you can effectively ban exports of a small device that can be carried in a suitcase. Chinese companies need it to train their frontier models and to compare with their home-developed chips.

I think the real threat is not the smuggling of advanced AI Nvidia chips. It is the strategy the U.S. government has been playing under administrations from both parties. As it goes without saying in the Tao Te Ching, the key levers of state power must be kept hidden from view.

True strategic assets, whether national military capabilities, core technologies, or vital levers of influence, are most effective when kept hidden, as quiet, unseen leverage. No one denies U.S. leadership in AI chips. But by restricting access so aggressively, it also pushes others, especially China, to develop their own systems that no longer need U.S. inputs.

Eventually, that could diminish U.S. leverage. That is the dynamic we are likely to see in the foreseeable future.

Riding ferries around New York for 13 hours changed my perspective on a city I’ve reported on and called home for nearly 30 years. Water covers roughly a third of the area of New York City; by day’s end, the city’s rivers, bays, inlets, straits, and channels felt less like barriers to cross and more like the connective tissue knitting the city together. 

We covered over 60 miles by boat — one-twelfth the distance to Bermuda! — all on a $15 pass.”

Inside his mansion were the owners "important things" china, artwork, and other remnants of former glory days. Not much mention of the slaves whose work enabled the owners riches. In fact, one "replica" of a slave cabin and not much discussion of the folks enslaved here.  As I took a walking path to a nearby waters edge. I thought to myself, here was the place where humans were "sold down the river".  I pledged to never visit another " plantation" again.
